tooltip.title: The skin may reveal the systemic diagnosis
tooltip.markdown: Use phenotype and history to target—not indiscriminately expand—the systemic evaluation.

tooltip.title: High-yield in Sweet/PG
tooltip.markdown: Myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myeloid leukemia, other myeloid neoplasms, plasma-cell dyscrasias, and monoclonal gammopathies. Bullous Sweet or dorsal-hand disease can be an important clue.

tooltip.title: PG and bowel-associated disease
tooltip.markdown: Ask about diarrhea, blood, abdominal pain, weight loss, perianal disease, and prior bowel surgery. PG can parallel or dissociate from intestinal activity.

tooltip.title: Broad overlap
tooltip.markdown: Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, Behçet syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, Schnitzler syndrome, CAPS, SAPHO, and vasculitis can produce neutrophilic or reactive granulomatous eruptions.

tooltip.title: Temporal causality matters
tooltip.markdown: G-CSF, all-trans retinoic acid, checkpoint inhibitors, targeted cancer therapy, antibiotics, and other medications can trigger Sweet-spectrum disease; avoid attributing causality without chronology and dechallenge context.

tooltip.title: Escalate by organ
tooltip.markdown: Eye, lung, bone, joint, bowel, nervous system, and other organs may be involved. New organ symptoms require targeted specialty evaluation rather than assuming all inflammation is cutaneous.

tooltip.title: Diagnosis is clinicopathologic
tooltip.markdown: Biopsy supports a neutrophilic pattern but is rarely disease-specific. Sample active untreated lesions, send tissue for microbial studies when infection is plausible, and interpret vasculitic change in relation to lesion age and clinical context.

tooltip.title: Plaque phenotype
tooltip.markdown: Abrupt tender plaques + dense upper-dermal neutrophils without primary leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Papillary dermal edema may create pseudovesiculation. Evaluate medication, malignancy, inflammatory disease, pregnancy, and infection triggers.

tooltip.title: Ulcer phenotype
tooltip.markdown: Biopsy the active ulcer edge deeply enough to include subcutis; the purpose is to support neutrophilic inflammation and exclude infection, vasculitis, malignancy, calciphylaxis, and other ulcer causes. A response to immunosuppression is supportive but not diagnostic.

tooltip.title: Urticarial phenotype
tooltip.markdown: Lesions are often less pruritic and more systemic than ordinary urticaria. Distinguish from urticarial vasculitis by duration, purpura/residual change, complement findings, and absence of fibrinoid vessel-wall necrosis.

tooltip.title: Papular/cord/plaque phenotype
tooltip.markdown: Early PNGD may show leukocytoclastic vasculitis and neutrophils around degenerated collagen; mature lesions show palisaded granulomas and fibrosis. IGD favors interstitial histiocytes around altered collagen, often without vasculitis.

tooltip.title: Do not skip
tooltip.markdown: Send bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial tissue cultures and special stains when morphology, host status, or severity makes infection plausible. Superficial swabs are inadequate for a deep necrotizing process.

tooltip.title: Pattern-based framework
tooltip.markdown: Neutrophilic dermatoses are sterile inflammatory disorders defined by compatible morphology and a neutrophil-predominant tissue reaction after infection and primary vasculitis have been appropriately excluded. Their phenotypes overlap and may represent a spectrum.

tooltip.title: Sweet-spectrum
tooltip.markdown: Abrupt tender erythematous-to-violaceous papules or plaques, often pseudovesicular because of papillary dermal edema; fever and neutrophilia may accompany classic Sweet syndrome.

tooltip.title: Pyoderma gangrenosum spectrum
tooltip.markdown: Rapidly progressive painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined border, pathergy, cribriform scarring, and associated IBD, inflammatory arthritis, hematologic disease, or monoclonal gammopathy.

tooltip.title: Neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis
tooltip.markdown: Nonpruritic or burning macules/thin plaques lasting <24–48 hours, often with fever or arthralgia; histology shows interstitial neutrophils and leukocytoclasia without true vasculitis or marked dermal edema.

tooltip.title: Reactive granulomatous dermatitis
tooltip.markdown: PNGD, IGD, and related reactive granulomatous patterns are associated with rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, vasculitis, malignancy, infection, and drugs; morphology and histology vary with lesion age.

tooltip.title: Safety-critical
tooltip.markdown: Sweet syndrome or pyoderma gangrenosum can mimic necrotizing infection, especially postoperatively or after G-CSF. Infection remains the default emergency until adequately evaluated; cultures, imaging, surgery, pathology, and clinical trajectory must be integrated.

tooltip.title: Control inflammation while protecting against missed infection
tooltip.markdown: Treatment depends on phenotype, severity, associated disease, and diagnostic certainty. Wound care and pain control are active treatments, not ancillary details.

tooltip.title: Often glucocorticoid-responsive
tooltip.markdown: Systemic glucocorticoid is typical for widespread or symptomatic disease; potent topical or intralesional corticosteroid may suffice for limited disease. Colchicine, dapsone, or other steroid-sparing therapy can be used for recurrent disease.

tooltip.title: Inflammation + wound strategy
tooltip.markdown: Gentle wound care, analgesia, avoidance of unnecessary trauma, and treatment of associated disease. Systemic glucocorticoid or ciclosporin are established initial choices; biologic or other immunosuppression is selected for refractory or associated-disease phenotypes.

tooltip.title: Target the driver
tooltip.markdown: Dapsone or colchicine may improve neutrophilic skin disease. IL-1 blockade can be highly effective when an IL-1–mediated systemic disorder is present.

tooltip.title: Treat underlying disease
tooltip.markdown: Optimize control of RA, lupus, vasculitis, malignancy, infection, or drug trigger. Topical/intralesional corticosteroid, hydroxychloroquine, dapsone, and selected systemic agents are case-dependent.

tooltip.title: Reopen the differential
tooltip.markdown: Progression despite appropriate immunosuppression should prompt renewed cultures, repeat/deeper biopsy, medication review, and reassessment for infection, vasculopathy, malignancy, or an alternative inflammatory ulcer.
